questions.subject: Reading
questions.learningObjective: Locate precise factual details in workplace instructions and answer within the stated word limit.
questions.prompt: Using no more than three words from the text, state where visiting instructors submit a loan request.
questions.passage:
Equipment loans for visiting instructors

A visiting instructor must submit a loan request through the staff portal. The office usually replies within two working days. If the requested item is unavailable, the reply will give a date on which a substitute can be collected.

Collect all approved equipment at the service desk on the ground floor. Bring your staff card and check the inventory slip before leaving. Any fault you spot at collection should be written on the inventory slip.

For an extended loan, request additional days through the portal before the original return date. When a loan ends outside desk hours, leave the sealed case in the return locker. It gives you a receipt, which you should keep until staff confirm the loan is closed.
questions.explanation: The first sentence names the staff portal as the place to submit the request.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.learningObjective: Identify each paragraph’s main idea and match it to a heading while distinguishing it from supporting details.
questions.prompt: Which heading best captures the main reason the museum kept the workbench in paragraph A? Write its Roman numeral.
questions.passage:
What became of the workbench?

A. When the town of Moorbridge closed its adult evening school, the woodwork room was cleared. Most equipment was catalogued by make or date before being offered to other schools. One heavy bench resisted such easy description. Its surface bore dozens of roughly parallel marks, and nobody knew which class had used it longest. The museum took the bench because the marks seemed to preserve evidence that the official records had missed.

B. At first, the museum planned to restore the top to its original appearance. A conservator changed that decision by showing a set of small holes that formed several regular patterns. Rather than damage to be erased, the holes indicated where different sorts of tools had been fixed. The team cleaned gently around them, preserving irregularities that an ordinary repair might have removed.

C. Photographs and class lists confirmed that the school had offered courses, but they said little about how people worked together. Former learners filled some gaps during recorded conversations. One described taking turns at the bench when space was short, while another remembered how experienced classmates demonstrated unfamiliar methods. Their accounts gave a clearer picture of the informal teaching the room had supported.

D. To put the bench on display, the museum had to solve a practical problem: it was too wide for the doorway to the usual gallery. The staff measured the available entrances and chose a smaller exhibition room that could be reached through a side corridor. That decision affected how visitors moved between displays, and the museum redrew its floor plan to make the new route visible.

E. The display originally ended with a label stating the last year of classes. After watching visitors, staff noticed that many began describing marks on objects from their own homes. They replaced the final label with a station where people could sketch one of those marks and explain what might have caused it. The exhibition thus began collecting new examples of the same kind of evidence that had made the bench worth keeping.

Headings
i. Personal accounts explain how learning took place
ii. Visitors become contributors
iii. A transport constraint changes the exhibition layout
iv. Keeping traces instead of removing them
v. A familiar object offers unusual evidence
vi. A dispute about the true age of the bench
vii. A school reopens after an exhibition
questions.explanation: The marks made the ordinary bench evidence of activities missing from the records.
